raw_response:
Four candidates could help express filtered or nested list construction concisely.

1. Haskell 98 list comprehensions — https://www.inf.ufes.br/~raulh/ufes/teaching/courses/ds/haskell/haskell98-report/exps.html
An output expression combined with generators and Boolean guards provides a direct model for concise list construction with selection and dependent nested iteration. The original report's title page is dated 1 February 1999 (https://www.inf.ufes.br/~raulh/ufes/teaching/courses/ds/haskell/haskell98-report/index.html), and the expression grammar was opened. Detailed section reads then failed; the semantics were cross-checked against the opened Haskell 1.3 section 3.11 (https://www.altocumulus.org/haskell-report/exps.html), which describes depth-first generators and a translation through map, filter, concatenation, and conditionals. Transfer requires explicit choices about eagerness, variable scope, and failed pattern matches. The 1999 section's detailed verification remains incomplete.

2. Common Lisp LOOP collect/append with conditional clauses — https://www.cs.cmu.edu/Groups/AI/util/html/cltl/clm/node246.html
LOOP's iteration clauses, conditional collection, and list-valued append clauses show how to return a filtered, transformed list without manual accumulator management. The opened section includes conditional collect examples and explains list concatenation. Its parent book identifies the source as the 1990 second edition (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/Groups/AI/html/cltl/cltl2.html). Multiple for clauses can advance inputs together; nested traversal therefore needs nested loops or appended inner results. Destructive nconc should be distinguished from ordinary list construction.

3. SRFI 1 filter-map and append-map combinators — https://srfi.schemers.org/srfi-1/srfi-1.html
Combining filter-map with nested append-map offers a library-level mechanism for conditional element generation and flattening repeated inner traversals into a new list. The public reference implementation was opened and its mapping definitions inspected: https://github.com/scheme-requests-for-implementation/srfi-1/blob/master/srfi-1-reference.scm. A design must account for filter-map dropping false results, unspecified function-call order, and multiple list arguments being traversed together rather than forming a Cartesian product automatically. The original specification records finalization on 9 October 1999, but the retrieved page includes errata through 3 October 2026; this run conservatively flags that specification evidence as post-decision and leaves the live source revision date unknown.

4. Erlang list comprehensions and generator-variable scope — https://www.erlang.org/docs/25/programming_examples/list_comprehensions.html
Erlang's list expression combines multiple generators and filters while defining local generator bindings, providing a concrete model for nested list construction and variable-scope decisions. The opened guide illustrates Cartesian products and explains that generator variables are fresh and do not escape the comprehension. Pattern matching and variable binding would need adaptation. This is later evidence: the opened documentation is for OTP 25, whose official release announcement is dated 18 May 2022 (https://www.erlang.org/news/157); no claim is made about the feature's first introduction.

These are transfer candidates, not claims of deployment or demonstrated usefulness. Public unauthenticated code search at https://grep.app/api/search?q=%28define%20%28filter-map succeeded with HTTP 200 and reported 33 matches; no native-search fallback was necessary. The search for an SQL alternative returned no visible PostgreSQL-specific result, so it did not yield a candidate. Failed document reads and uncertain dates are retained in the evidence log. The run used six search query strings and conservatively counted twenty page-read attempts, including find operations, failed requests, and revisits.
